reader_summary.overview: Wilfred Frost talks to financial historian Edward Chancellor about the psychology behind market bubbles. They review major historical events like Tulip Mania and the Dot-Com crash to show why crowd delusion repeats itself. The discussion highlights that modern technology spreads irrationality faster, but smart investors wait for the crash to find true winners.

notes: We’re in a bubble. It will burst. And there are lessons from history that make all that clear. In this episode of The Master Investor Podcast, Wilfred Frost sits down with renowned financial historian and author of Devil Take the Hindmost, Edward Chancellor, for an timely deep dive into market manias, moral hazard, and the psychology of crowd delusion. Drawing striking parallels across 400 years – from 17th-century Tulip Mania, the South Sea Bubble in the 1720s, to the 1840s British Railway craze and the Dot-Com crash – Chancellor reveals why human nature never changes, why modern hyper-connectivity makes market irrationality spread faster than ever, and why the smart money always waits for the post-bubble shakeout before picking the true long-term winners. Wilf and Edward review all of the major bubbles of the last 400 years, and draw out the themes that are relevant today, including the fact that “the number one feature of when a speculative bubble bursts is tighter money”; why most bubbles feature a Messianic leader, like Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, Sam Altman or Dario Amodei – “Every mania is more efficient when it's organised Around a leader who generates a huge degree of confidence”; and how the long term winners of technological revolutions usually materialise after the shakeout, and thus “it makes sense to stand back, wait for the bubble burst, and then see which companies appear to be gathering a dominant position.” Recorded 9th November 2026 00:00 Intro 05:24 Three stages of a bubble 07:41 Social aspect of bubbles 10:00 Investing vs gambling 12:11 Tulip mania & early 1600s 15:02 1690s – first contrarians 19:00 South Sea Bubble 1720s 21:14 Momentum vs Greater Fool 25:00 Messianic leaders today vs Sir John Blunt in South Sea Bubble 29:12 Midterms – mirrors of history? 32:06 Railway mania 1840s vs today 36:15 1920s: radio, tickers and how faster information fuels speculation 40:33 Japan 1980s & moral hazard 43:23 Dot-com bubble vs today 47:09 Real winners emerge after bubble bursts 49:01 Bubble aspects today 52:24 Government debt makes things worse 55:00 History gives confidence this is a bubble 56:40 Rising rates pops bubbles 59:45 Avoid passive index investing Watch the full episode on The Master Investor Podcast YouTube channel Follow @WilfredFrost on X and Linked In And NEW: Subscribe to The Master Investor Podcast Memos You can also find Edward’s own podcast - The Capital Cycle Podcast - here: https://www.thecapitalcycle.co.uk/ Sponsored by BNY Investments, Interactive Brokers - ibkr.com/masterinvestor, The World Gold Council and London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG).  In this episode of The Master Investor Podcast , Wilfred Frost sits down with renowned financial historian and author of Devil Take the Hindmost , Edward Chancellor, for an timely deep dive into market manias, moral hazard, and the psychology of crowd delusion. 

 Drawing striking parallels across 400 years – from 17th-century Tulip Mania, the South Sea Bubble in the 1720s, to the 1840s British Railway craze and the Dot-Com crash – Chancellor reveals why human nature never changes, why modern hyper-connectivity makes market irrationality spread faster than ever, and why the smart money always waits for the post-bubble shakeout before picking the true long-term winners. 

 Wilf and Edward review all of the major bubbles of the last 400 years, and draw out the themes that are relevant today, including the fact that “the number one feature of when a speculative bubble bursts is tighter money”; why most bubbles feature a Messianic leader, like Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, Sam Altman or Dario Amodei – “Every mania is more efficient when it's organised Around a leader who generates a huge degree of confidence”; and how the long term winners of technological revolutions usually materialise after the shakeout, and thus “it makes sense to stand back, wait for the bubble burst, and then see which companies appear to be gathering a dominant position.”
